alt: Question 1, worth 5 marks, asks short questions on both sources; Question 2 works on the evidence in one source; Question 3 is an essay comparing both. Five of the paper’s 45 marks is about one-ninth, roughly 10 of the 90 minutes.
caption: About ten minutes, but the close reading you do here feeds Questions 2 and 3.

alt: Ten statement types with a working definition and typical signal words: fact, opinion, argument, rant, speculation, prediction, explanation, hypothesis, account and belief. Argument and explanation are highlighted because both use “because”.
caption: Classify a sentence by what it is doing, using the signals as clues, not proof.

alt: An argument uses “because” to persuade you of a conclusion, while an explanation uses it to say why something accepted is so. A checkable statement about park temperature is a claim of fact: it can be identified as a fact-type statement, but whether to accept it is a matter of evaluation.
caption: Persuading or explaining? Checkable or checked? Ask both before you label.

after: ## Skill 2: locating the parts of an argument
alt: An argument map: reasons and supporting evidence lead to an intermediate conclusion, which supports the main conclusion. An unstated assumption is a missing step the argument needs, and a counter-assertion is a view raised in order to be answered.
caption: Find the claim everything else supports, then name the role of each other sentence.

alt: A comparison names a point of comparison, then states Source A’s and Source B’s position on it, as in the example where both accept streets are hotter than parks but differ on tree planting and fairness. Comparing at topic level, “both are about cities”, earns little.
caption: Name the point, then each source’s position on it.

alt: Source A’s three sentences labelled: the 8 °C temperature figure is a claim of fact used as evidence, the plan to plant 20,000 trees by 2030 is the main conclusion and a prediction, and the claim that trees are the cheapest option is an unsupported assertion. Source B’s perspective differs by judging who benefits first.
caption: Three sentences, three different kinds of statement: that precision earns the marks.

alt: Four command words with what each asks: identify means name, select or recognise, using the source’s words; explain means set out reasons, in your own words; compare covers similarities and differences, contrast only differences, both naming the two sources together.
caption: Identify in the source’s words; explain in your own.
